title: How Dog Training Works
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck discuss dog training, contrasting the dominance theory approach with positive reinforcement. They cover the origins of dominance theory in captive wolf studies (Rudolph Schenkel, L. David Mech's later revision), physical and psychological dominance techniques (alpha roll, dominance down, scruff shake, leash jerk, choke/pinch/shock collars, staring), the fear-and-aggression problem with punishment, the operant conditioning categories (positive/negative reinforcement and punishment), the least intrusive minimally aversive hierarchy, and positive reinforcement methods like extinction, ignoring unwanted behavior, and clicker training. They discuss a 2009 survey on physical punishment and aggression, the criticism of Cesar Millan and the National Geographic pig incident, and common behavior misreadings like jumping, pulling on leash, and house soiling. The episode ends with a listener mail from Chandra in San Diego about her great-great-grandfather William Harvey Beal's barbed wire tightener.

segments.title: Opening banter on dog training
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on dog training, sharing anecdotes about their own dogs such as Nico's excitement when guests arrive and the difficulty of training it out.

segments.title: Dominance versus positive reinforcement
segments.summary: The hosts contrast the two main approaches: dominance, which discourages unwanted behavior, and positive reinforcement, which rewards desired behavior. They note that ignoring a dog or scolding it can reinforce bad behavior.

segments.title: Origins of dominance theory in wolf studies
segments.summary: Dominance theory is based on the idea that dogs are like wolves and that wolf packs have alpha leaders. The hosts describe the New Skete monks and early captive-wolf studies, and David Mech's later field research and revision of his earlier views, which showed alphas are better understood as parents.

segments.title: Physical and psychological dominance techniques
segments.summary: The hosts describe techniques recommended by dominance trainers: the alpha roll, dominance down, scruff shake, leash jerk, choke, pinch, and shock collars, and staring or growling. They also discuss how dog fights are broken up and how fear can underlie aggression.

segments.title: Problems with dominance training and the punishment hierarchy
segments.summary: The hosts explain that dominance training can suppress behavior but may shut dogs down and increase fear and aggression. They discuss least intrusive minimally aversive training, the four operant conditioning quadrants including positive punishment, and B. F. Skinner's view that positive punishment is least effective.

segments.title: Common behavior misreadings and the first steps
segments.summary: The hosts list health checks, such as a vet visit for house soiling, and environment changes as early steps. They walk through misread behaviors like jumping, pulling on leash, and running through doorways, and explain how dominance and positive reinforcement readings differ.

segments.title: Research on physical punishment, Cesar Millan, and criticism
segments.summary: The hosts describe a 2009 survey finding that physically punished dogs often responded with aggression, and professional dog training organizations rejecting dominance methods. They discuss Cesar Millan's show, the National Geographic pig incident, and his continued support for dominance training.

segments.title: Positive reinforcement: extinction and clicker training
segments.summary: The hosts explain extinction, where unwanted behavior is ignored and desired behavior is rewarded consistently, and describe clicker training as a way to mark the exact behavior. They stress consistency and say that furniture rules are a matter of household choice.

segments.title: Listener mail: barbed wire tightener
segments.summary: Listener Chandra from San Diego writes that her great-great-grandfather William Harvey Beal invented a barbed wire tightener and sold it across the West.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank the listener and give contact information for the show.
